before.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

before.label: Practice theory
before.description: Examines how embodied dispositions and situated activities reproduce or alter social relations. Bourdieu’s habitus and strategies, de Certeau’s tactics, and Sewell’s account of structure offer different ways to connect agency, constraint, and meaning. These are several resources for reassessing cultural history, not a single replacement paradigm.

after.scope_note: Bourdieu, de Certeau, and Sewell offer distinct accounts. Practice theory is not a unified successor to cultural history. Collaborative everyday research, cultural repertoires and Ortner’s plural orientation broaden this selection. Strategy has different meanings across these authors.

before.label: Norbert Elias
before.description: Links changes in manners and affect to interdependence and state formation. Historians adapt and contest his account of the relations between social constraint and self-restraint. The approach raises questions about historical scale and variation rather than supplying a universal ladder of civilization.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Über den Prozeß der Zivilisation (1939), known in English as The Civilizing Process; The Court Society (German 1969). Distinguish original publication, translations, and later reception.
before.scope_note: Interdependence, manners, and state formation are historical questions; comparison with Weber or Freud is not automatically demonstrated borrowing.

after.label: Norbert Elias

after.representative_figures_and_works: Über den Prozeß der Zivilisation (1939), known in English as The Civilizing Process; The Court Society (German 1969). Distinguish original publication, translations, and later reception.
after.scope_note: Interdependence, manners, and state formation are historical questions; comparison with Weber or Freud is not automatically demonstrated borrowing. His retrospective interview names psychoanalytic and Durkheimian readings. Collaborative projects and Duerr’s criticism qualify the range of this inquiry; book bodies and reception are checked separately.

before.label: Comparative historical sociology
before.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Barrington Moore, Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966); Theda Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (1979); Charles Tilly; Michael Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986); Perry Anderson (1974).
